regions.name: Provence
regions.summary: Provence is the rosé region of France: about nine bottles in ten are pale, dry and pink, blended from Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah with Mourvèdre and the local Tibouren. Côtes de Provence is the large appellation, Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence and Coteaux Varois en Provence the two other broad ones, and a ring of small historic appellations holds the character: Bandol for Mourvèdre reds that age, Cassis for white, Bellet above Nice, Palette near Aix and Les Baux-de-Provence in the Alpilles. The climate is Mediterranean, the mistral dries the western half and limestone gives way to schist and granite in the east. A server holds Bandol equals Mourvèdre, the rosé grapes and the 1955 crus classés.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean: long hot summers, mild winters and close to three thousand hours of sunshine a year, with rain falling mostly in spring and autumn storms. The mistral blows cold and dry down the Rhône corridor across the western half, cooling the vines and keeping rot away but breaking shoots. Nearer the coast sea breezes temper the heat, and inland the Var hills climb into cooler nights. Drought, water stress and forest fire are the modern hazards.
terroir.soils: The west, from the Alpilles through Aix, Sainte-Victoire, Cassis and Bandol, is limestone and clay-limestone country, often as bare white rock and scree. East of a line near Toulon the old crystalline massifs take over: the Maures and the Esterel bring schist, gneiss, granite and red porphyry, giving the darker, more mineral rosés of the coast. Bandol's terraces mix limestone with sandstone and marl, and Bellet sits on a pebbly conglomerate above Nice.
terroir.topography: An arc of hills and short mountain ridges between the Rhône delta and the Italian border: the Alpilles, the Sainte-Victoire and Sainte-Baume ridges, the Maures along the coast and the Esterel at Fréjus. The vineyards sit in valleys and on terraced slopes, the restanques, and in the natural amphitheatres that open to the sea at Bandol and Cassis. Pierrevert, in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, is the highest and coolest.
terroir.water: The Mediterranean runs the whole southern edge and moderates the coast; the Rhône marks the west and the Durance crosses the north. Bandol's bay faces due south, which is what lets Mourvèdre ripen.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: The body and the strawberry fruit of most rosé and of the reds of Aix, Les Baux and the Var; bush trained and drought hardy.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: The rosé grape above all: pale, soft, low in tannin, bringing delicacy and a redcurrant lift to the blend.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Colour, pepper and structure in reds and a share of the rosé blends, strongest in the cooler inland Var.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Bandol's grape, at least half of every red there: dark, meaty, tannic and slow, with the sea's warmth needed to ripen it.

grapes.name: Tibouren
grapes.styles: Provence's own rosé speciality, the same vine as Liguria's Rossese and scarcely grown elsewhere in France: delicate, herbal and pale, prized on the coast around Saint-Tropez.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: Called Rolle here; the main white grape, dry, citrus and fennel, and a small lifting share of many rosés.

grapes.name: Clairette
grapes.styles: A traditional white of Cassis, Palette and the hills: low in acid, floral and full.

grapes.name: Marsanne
grapes.styles: Leads the white of Cassis with Clairette and Ugni Blanc, giving weight and a honeyed edge.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Permitted in Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence and Les Baux-de-Provence as a blending partner for Syrah and Grenache; Trévallon's half-Cabernet red left the appellation for the IGP over its share.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Old vines survive in the Var; capped in most appellation blends and fading.

grapes.name: Braquet
grapes.styles: A Bellet grape for perfumed rosé and light red, with Folle Noire for the deeper reds of that one hillside.

wines.note: Pale salmon, dry, light and crisp: strawberry, peach, citrus and a herbal note of garrigue. Serve cold at 8 to 10 degrees with grilled fish, salade niçoise, bouillabaisse and the whole of summer.
Mourvèdre-led, deep, tannic and savoury, black fruit, leather and herbs after eighteen months in large oak; it wants years in bottle and lamb, game or daube at the table.
Fuller, more structured and more savoury than the Var norm because Mourvèdre is in it; it keeps a few years and takes grilled meat and spiced fish.
Dry, full and gently saline from Marsanne, Clairette and Ugni Blanc, fennel and white flowers; the wine for bouillabaisse and the calanques.
Grenache and Syrah with Cabernet Sauvignon allowed: medium bodied, herbal and ripe, for grilled lamb and ratatouille.
Red and rosé from the Alpilles, Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre with some Cabernet, mostly organic, and a little white since 2011; the reds are dark and warm.
A rarity near Aix in all three colours, oak aged, made from a long list of old local grapes; the white is nutty and long lived.
From the hills above Nice: rosé and light red from Braquet and Folle Noire, white from Rolle; tiny and almost all drunk on the Riviera.

made.viticulture: Grenache and Mourvèdre were traditionally bush vines, en gobelet, low to the ground against the mistral, and old vines stay that way; most of the rosé vineyard is now trained on wires in cordon de Royat or Guyot so that machines can pick fast at night and bring cool fruit to the press. Picking for rosé comes early, before the sugars climb, since the style wants moderate alcohol and acidity. The dry air keeps mildew and rot down, which is why organic farming is so widespread here. The hazards are drought and water stress in the hot years, with irrigation tightly limited, the mistral snapping young shoots in the west, late spring frost in the inland valleys and summer fire in the pine and scrub. At Bandol the vines stand on stone-walled terraces in a south-facing amphitheatre, picked by hand, and Mourvèdre is planted where the sea's heat reaches it, because it ripens later than anything around it; the rules require at least half of a red to be Mourvèdre, and most growers go well above that.
made.winemaking: Rosé is the craft. The two routes are direct pressing of whole grapes, which gives the palest wine, and a few hours of skin contact before the juice is drawn off, the saignée; either way the point is to take colour and little tannin. The juice is settled cold, fermented cool in stainless steel, usually kept from malolactic conversion to hold the freshness, sometimes left on fine lees for texture, and bottled within months, since the wine is meant for the coming summer. Blending is the rule: Côtes de Provence rosé must combine grapes, never one alone, and Rolle may add a white lift. The Centre du Rosé at Vidauban, founded in 1999, is the research station that set the colour scale and the modern style. The reds of Bandol are the opposite temper: Mourvèdre, Grenache and Cinsault go through long maceration and then at least eighteen months in wood, traditionally large old foudres, before sale, emerging tannic and reductive and built for a decade. Cassis and Palette whites are fermented dry and often rested in old wood; at Palette, Château Simone rests its wines in old wood for years.

law.classification: Nine appellations and a wide IGP net. Côtes de Provence, created in 1977, is by far the largest, running across the Var into the Bouches-du-Rhône and a corner of the Alpes-Maritimes, and carries five named sub-zones that may follow its name on the label: Sainte-Victoire and Fréjus from 2005, La Londe from 2008, Pierrefeu from 2013 and Notre-Dame des Anges from 2019. Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence (1985) covers the west and Coteaux Varois en Provence (1993) the centre. The small historic appellations are Cassis (1936), Bandol and Bellet (1941), Palette (1948), Les Baux-de-Provence (1995) and Pierrevert (1998). Inside Côtes de Provence a classification of 1955 named twenty-three estates Cru Classé; the title belongs to the land, cannot be won anew and is still used by most of them. Below the appellations sit IGP Méditerranée, IGP Var, IGP Bouches-du-Rhône and IGP Alpilles, where growers such as Trévallon work outside the appellation grape rules.
tiers: Côtes de Provence AOC

places.name: Côtes de Provence
places.note: The great rosé appellation from the Var coast to the hills behind Saint-Tropez and the slopes of Sainte-Victoire, with Minuty at Gassin and Esclans at La Motte-en-Provence among its best-known estates.

places.name: Sainte-Victoire
places.note: Limestone slopes under the mountain painted by Cézanne, east of Aix; a sub-zone since 2005 for red and rosé.

places.name: Fréjus
places.note: Volcanic and crystalline soils of the Esterel on the eastern coast; a sub-zone since 2005, Tibouren at home here.

places.name: La Londe
places.note: Schist by the sea near Hyères, a sub-zone since 2008 and the only one of the five with a white beside its mineral rosé and red.

places.name: Pierrefeu and Notre-Dame des Anges
places.note: The two inland sub-zones of the central Var, added in 2013 and 2019, the second the most recent of the five as of 2026.

places.name: Vidauban
places.note: The village in the Var holding the Centre du Rosé, the research station that defined the pale modern style.

places.name: Bandol
places.note: A south-facing amphitheatre of terraces around the fishing port west of Toulon, across La Cadière-d'Azur, Le Castellet, Saint-Cyr-sur-Mer and their neighbours: Mourvèdre reds of real age, a serious rosé and a little white.

places.name: Le Plan du Castellet
places.note: The hamlet below Le Castellet where Domaine Tempier set the standard for Mourvèdre after the appellation came in 1941.

places.name: La Cadière-d'Azur
places.note: The hilltop village whose high limestone terraces hold Pibarnon and some of the appellation's coolest sites.

places.name: Cassis
places.note: The small calanque port east of Marseille, an appellation of 1936 and the region's white-wine name: Marsanne, Clairette and Ugni Blanc on limestone above the sea.

places.name: Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence
places.note: The western appellation around Aix and the Durance, limestone and the mistral, red and rosé with Cabernet Sauvignon allowed beside Grenache and Syrah.

places.name: Les Baux-de-Provence and the Alpilles
places.note: The jagged limestone ridge north of Arles: an appellation since 1995, almost wholly organic, red and rosé with white admitted in 2011, and the IGP Alpilles beside it, where Domaine de Trévallon makes its Cabernet and Syrah red and a Marsanne-led white at Saint-Étienne-du-Grès.

places.name: Palette
places.note: A few hillsides at Meyreuil just east of Aix, an appellation since 1948 dominated by Château Simone: oak-aged red, white and rosé from a long roll of old varieties.

places.name: Bellet
places.note: Terraces in the hills behind Nice on pebbly conglomerate, an appellation since 1941: Braquet and Folle Noire for rosé and red, Rolle for white.

places.name: Coteaux Varois en Provence
places.note: The centre of the Var around Brignoles, higher and cooler than the coast, an appellation since 1993; the rosés are a touch firmer.

places.name: Pierrevert
places.note: The highest Provence appellation, in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence near Manosque, since 1998; fresher wines in all three colours.

producers.name: Domaine Tempier
producers.why: The reference for Bandol red and rosé, the estate that built the appellation's name on Mourvèdre.

producers.name: Château de Pibarnon
producers.why: High limestone terraces at La Cadière-d'Azur giving the most elegant, long-lived Bandol.

producers.name: Château Pradeaux
producers.why: Saint-Cyr-sur-Mer traditionalist whose Bandol reds are near pure Mourvèdre and need a decade.

producers.name: Domaines Ott
producers.why: The house that made Provence rosé a luxury, with crus classés at Château de Selle and Clos Mireille and a Bandol estate.

producers.name: Château Minuty
producers.why: Cru Classé at Gassin on the Saint-Tropez peninsula; its pale rosés are on lists worldwide.

producers.name: Château d'Esclans
producers.why: La Motte-en-Provence estate behind Whispering Angel and the oak-fermented Garrus, the wines that priced rosé upward.

producers.name: Château Simone
producers.why: Nearly the whole of Palette: foudre-aged white, red and rosé from very old vines.

producers.name: Domaine de Trévallon
producers.why: The Alpilles estate whose Cabernet and Syrah red is bottled as IGP because the appellation caps Cabernet.

exam: Bandol: Mourvèdre at least half the red, eighteen months in wood.
The rosé blend: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Tibouren, and Rolle as the white.
Côtes de Provence as the largest appellation and its five named sub-zones.
Cassis for white wine; Bellet and Palette as the two tiny ones.
The 1955 crus classés of Côtes de Provence, a title that cannot be gained.
How pale rosé is made: direct press or short maceration, cool fermentation, no malolactic.
West against east: limestone and mistral against schist and granite.
traps: Cassis the appellation is dry white wine from a port near Marseille; crème de cassis is the blackcurrant liqueur of Burgundy.
Bandol makes a fine rosé, but the exam's Bandol answer is Mourvèdre red.
Cru Classé in Provence is a 1955 list of estates inside Côtes de Provence, nothing to do with 1855.
Rolle and Vermentino are the same grape under two names.
Palette and Bellet are appellations, not villages or grapes, and each is smaller than the largest Médoc estates.
Pale colour is a style choice from early picking and direct pressing, not a sign of a thin wine.
Les Baux-de-Provence is in Provence; Costières de Nîmes, just across the Rhône delta, belongs to the Rhône.

cards.f: Bandol red: what the law requires
cards.b: Mourvèdre at least 50 per cent, usually far more, with Grenache and Cinsault; at least eighteen months in wood before sale.
Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre and Tibouren, with Rolle (Vermentino) as a white lift; always a blend.

cards.f: The three broad appellations of Provence
cards.b: Côtes de Provence (the largest), Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence (west), Coteaux Varois en Provence (centre).

cards.f: The five sub-zones of Côtes de Provence
cards.b: Sainte-Victoire and Fréjus (2005), La Londe (2008), Pierrefeu (2013), Notre-Dame des Anges (2019).
A port near Marseille making mostly dry white from Marsanne, Clairette and Ugni Blanc; among the first appellations, 1936. Not the liqueur.
A 1955 classification of twenty-three Côtes de Provence estates; it stays with the land and cannot be won today.

cards.f: The two tiny appellations of Provence: where each lies
cards.b: Bellet, in the hills behind Nice (Braquet, Folle Noire, Rolle), and Palette, just east of Aix, led by Château Simone (oak-aged, all three colours).
Direct press or a few hours of skin contact, cold settling, cool steel fermentation, malolactic blocked, early bottling.
West: limestone, mistral, Aix, Bandol, Cassis. East: schist, granite and porphyry of the Maures and Esterel.
The Provençal name for Vermentino, the region's main white grape.

questions.q: Which grape must make up at least half of a red Bandol?
questions.exp: Bandol red is built on Mourvèdre, at least 50 per cent by law and usually more, with Grenache and Cinsault as partners; Syrah is allowed only as a small accessory grape.

questions.q: Which Provence appellation is known above all for its dry white wine?
questions.exp: Cassis, a port near Marseille, is the region's white-wine appellation, from Marsanne, Clairette and Ugni Blanc. Bandol is Mourvèdre red, the other two are red and rosé country.

questions.q: In which year were the Côtes de Provence crus classés ranked?
questions.exp: Twenty-three estates were classified in 1955. 1855 is the Médoc, 1936 the first appellations including Cassis, and 1977 the creation of the Côtes de Provence appellation itself.

questions.q: Which grape is Provence's own rosé speciality, scarcely grown anywhere else in France?
questions.exp: Tibouren is the local variety, delicate and herbal, at home around Saint-Tropez and Fréjus, and the same vine as Liguria's Rossese. The other three are grown across the whole of southern France.

questions.q: Under what name is Vermentino grown and labelled in Provence?
questions.exp: Vermentino goes by Rolle in Provence and the Languedoc, and the name appears on labels; it is the region's main white grape and gives many rosés a citrus lift.

questions.q: Which appellation in the hills above Nice grows Braquet and Folle Noire?
questions.exp: Bellet is the tiny appellation of the Nice hills, with Braquet and Folle Noire for its rosé and red and Rolle for its white.

questions.q: How long must a red Bandol spend in wood before it can be sold?
questions.exp: Bandol's rules require at least eighteen months in wood, traditionally large old foudres, which is part of why the reds taste reductive and tannic on release.

questions.q: Which small appellation just east of Aix-en-Provence is the home of Château Simone?
questions.exp: Palette, an appellation since 1948 on a few hillsides at Meyreuil, is led by Château Simone, which ages its red, white and rosé for years in old wood.

regions.name: Bordeaux
regions.summary: Bordeaux is the maritime blending region of south-western France, split by the Gironde estuary into a Left Bank of gravel where Cabernet Sauvignon leads and a Right Bank of clay and limestone where Merlot leads with Cabernet Franc. The Médoc communes run north from Margaux through Saint-Julien and Pauillac to Saint-Estèphe; Pessac-Léognan holds the gravel south of the city; Saint-Émilion and Pomerol face them across the water. Whites blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, dry at Pessac-Léognan and Entre-Deux-Mers, sweet at Sauternes, where the Ciron's mists bring noble rot. The 1855 classification froze the Médoc's five growths, Saint-Émilion reclassifies about every decade and Pomerol has no list at all.

terroir.climate: Maritime and moderate: the Atlantic keeps winters mild and summers warm rather than hot, and the pine forest of the Landes blunts the sea wind and the salt. Rain is the risk at every turn, spoiling flowering in June, bringing mildew through summer and threatening the picking in late September and October. Because no single grape can be relied on, the vineyard is planted to several that flower and ripen at different moments, and the cellar settles the blend each year.
terroir.soils: The Left Bank is deep gravel laid down by ancient rivers in low mounds, the croupes, which drain fast and store the day's warmth, letting late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon finish this far north. The Right Bank is cooler clay over limestone, with a limestone plateau at Saint-Émilion and blue clay at the top of Pomerol, ground that suits Merlot. Sauternes mixes gravel and sand over limestone, and Entre-Deux-Mers is clay and limestone hills.
terroir.topography: Low and open: a wide estuary plain on the Left Bank where a rise of a few metres in gravel decides a vineyard's rank, the hills of Entre-Deux-Mers between the two rivers, and the limestone escarpment and plateau of Saint-Émilion on the Right Bank, the only real slopes in the region.
terroir.water: The Garonne and the Dordogne meet north of the city to form the Gironde, the tidal estuary that moderates the whole region and divides its banks. The small, cold, spring-fed Ciron runs into the warmer Garonne at Barsac, in the Sauternes district, and the autumn mists where they meet breed the noble rot.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted grape and the backbone of the Right Bank and of everyday red: early ripening, plummy, soft and fleshy, prone to coulure at flowering.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The Left Bank leader on warm gravel: blackcurrant, cedar and graphite, firm tannin and long life, the last grape picked.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Perfume, red fruit and leafy freshness; a large share at Cheval Blanc and across Saint-Émilion, a seasoning in the Médoc.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A late-ripening dash of colour, spice and tannin in Médoc blends, rarely above a tenth.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Historic and now scarce, lingering in Bourg, Blaye and the Côtes; a legal variety that students forget.

grapes.name: Carmenère
grapes.styles: The old Médoc grape nearly lost to phylloxera and still permitted, planted by a few estates as a curiosity.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: Thin skinned and botrytis prone, the heart of Sauternes and the weight in dry white, waxy and honeyed with age.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Aroma and acidity for dry white at Entre-Deux-Mers and Pessac-Léognan, and the lift in sweet blends; Sauvignon Gris is its rarer cousin.

grapes.name: Muscadelle
grapes.styles: The third white, grapey and floral, a small seasoning in sweet and dry blends; no relation to Muscat.

wines.note: Cabernet-led: blackcurrant, cedar, pencil shavings and firm tannin, built for a decade or more; decant young bottles and serve at 17 degrees with lamb or beef.
Merlot with Cabernet Franc: plum, truffle and a softer, rounder grip, approachable sooner than the Médoc, for duck, mushrooms and braised dishes.
Merlot at its most plush: velvet tannin, black cherry, chocolate and iron, the smallest great appellation; roast meats and anything with truffle.
Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon fermented and aged in barrel: smoky, waxy, citrus and nut, long lived; for rich fish and lobster.
Dry, crisp, Sauvignon-led white from steel, the region's oyster wine; the appellation covers white only.
Botrytised Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc: apricot, honey, saffron and marmalade on bright acidity; serve cool with foie gras, Roquefort or on its own.
The region-wide red with a touch more ripeness and ageing than plain Bordeaux, Merlot-led and medium bodied; the Tuesday-night claret.
Traditional method sparkling, an appellation since 1990, mostly from Sémillon and Sauvignon; little seen outside the region.

made.viticulture: Vines are trained low on wires, most often Guyot double, and planted densely in the classed growths, around eight to ten thousand to the hectare on the gravel, so that each vine carries a small crop. The gravel mounds are prized because they drain and warm; a rise of two metres can separate a classed growth from its neighbour. Picking is by hand at the top and by machine across most of the generic appellations, Merlot first and Cabernet Sauvignon last. The hazards are rain at flowering, which causes coulure in Merlot and uneven set, downy mildew through a wet summer, hail, spring frost in the low-lying parts and rot before harvest; the copper and lime spray called Bordeaux mixture was devised here in the 1880s against mildew. Since 2021 the INAO has allowed Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur growers to plant six extra varieties on trial against a warming climate, among them Marselan, Touriga Nacional and Alvarinho, on no more than five per cent of the vineyard and ten per cent of a blend.
made.winemaking: Red grapes are destemmed and fermented in steel, concrete or oak vats with two to four weeks on the skins; malolactic conversion follows, in barrel at ambitious estates. The wine then rests twelve to twenty-four months in the 225-litre barrique, with new oak from a quarter to all of the barrels at the top, racked every few months and traditionally fined with egg white. The assemblage comes in the spring after harvest, when the cellar decides the proportions of each grape and which lots go into the grand vin and which into the second wine. Nearly everything is château bottled, sold through courtiers and négociants on the Place de Bordeaux and offered as futures, en primeur, while still in barrel. Dry whites at Pessac-Léognan are barrel fermented and stirred on their lees; Entre-Deux-Mers is made cold in steel. Sauternes is picked in several passes through the vineyard, the tries, taking only the shrivelled botrytised berries, pressed, fermented in barrel and stopped by sulphur or on its own; the finished wine must hold at least 45 grams of sugar per litre and ages for years in oak.

law.classification: The appellations run from the regional Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur, through the district names such as Médoc, Graves and Entre-Deux-Mers, to the communes: Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux, Listrac-Médoc and Moulis-en-Médoc in the Médoc, Pessac-Léognan in the Graves, Sauternes and Barsac for sweet wine, Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and Fronsac on the Right Bank. Over the appellations sit the estate classifications, each with its own logic. The 1855 list ranked sixty-one red estates, sixty of the Médoc and Haut-Brion, into five growths on price, and ranked Sauternes and Barsac separately under Yquem; it has moved once, when Mouton rose to First Growth in 1973. The Graves classification of 1953, confirmed in 1959, is a single tier of crus classés, all now in Pessac-Léognan, for red, white or both. Saint-Émilion first classified in 1955 and rewrites its list about every ten years; the 2022 edition named Figeac and Pavie Premier Grand Cru Classé A after Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus withdrew. Pomerol has never classified. The Cru Bourgeois du Médoc is a separate five-yearly list below the 1855 growths, last published on 10 February 2025 with 170 estates in three tiers.
tiers: Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur
The regional appellations covering the whole vineyard; Supérieur means slightly higher minimum alcohol, lower yields and longer ageing, not a quality rank.
District appellations
Médoc, Haut-Médoc, Graves, Entre-Deux-Mers (dry white only), Côtes de Bordeaux with its named communes.
Commune appellations
Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux, Listrac-Médoc, Moulis-en-Médoc, Pessac-Léognan, Sauternes, Barsac, Saint-Émilion and Saint-Émilion Grand Cru, Pomerol, Fronsac and Canon-Fronsac.
1855 Classification (Médoc and Sauternes)
Five growths of red, Premier to Cinquième Cru Classé: 5, 14, 14, 10 and 18 estates; Sauternes and Barsac in Premier Cru Supérieur (Yquem alone), Premier Cru and Deuxième Cru.
Graves Cru Classé
The 1953 and 1959 list of sixteen estates, one tier, red and white judged separately; all in Pessac-Léognan.
Saint-Émilion classification
Premier Grand Cru Classé A and B, then Grand Cru Classé, revised about every ten years, most recently in 2022; plain Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation, not a rank.
Cru Bourgeois du Médoc
Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel, Supérieur and Cru Bourgeois, revised every five years; 2020, then 10 February 2025 with 170 estates and 14 Exceptionnel.
Pomerol
No classification of any kind; Pétrus, Le Pin, Trotanoy and Lafleur are unranked.
labels: A classified estate: in the Médoc an 1855 growth, in Graves the 1959 list, in Saint-Émilion the current classification
A First Growth of 1855 or a Sauternes first growth
An appellation with lower yields and longer ageing than plain Saint-Émilion, not a classification
An estate's main wine, an unregulated phrase
The estate's second selection, from younger vines and declassified lots
A Médoc estate on the current five-yearly list below the 1855 growths
A small family Médoc estate on a separate list, first published in 2006 and revised since
A dark rosé, the colour of the medieval claret
Dry white from anywhere in the region; the dry wines of Sauternes estates such as Y of Yquem use it
A Sauternes commune that may label as Barsac or as Sauternes

places.name: Left Bank
places.note: The gravel side west of the Gironde and Garonne, Saint-Estèphe down to Sauternes: Cabernet country, the 1855 estates and the whites of the Graves.

places.name: Médoc
places.note: The peninsula north of the city; Haut-Médoc holds the six communes and Médoc AOC the flatter northern land, where Merlot gains as the gravel thins.

places.name: Saint-Estèphe
places.note: The northernmost commune, more clay and sturdier, slower wines: Cos d'Estournel and Montrose are Second Growths, Calon-Ségur a Third, Meyney unclassified.

places.name: Pauillac
places.note: Three First Growths, Lafite, Latour and Mouton, the two Pichons and Lynch-Bages: eighteen classed growths of pure cassis-and-cedar Cabernet.

places.name: Saint-Julien
places.note: No First Growth but five Seconds, the three Léovilles, Ducru-Beaucaillou and Gruaud Larose; the balanced midpoint of claret; Talbot and Beychevelle are Fourths.

places.name: Margaux
places.note: The southern commune of perfume and silk: Château Margaux the First, Palmer and d'Issan Thirds, Rauzan-Ségla and Brane-Cantenac Seconds; twenty-one classed growths, the most of any commune.

places.name: Listrac-Médoc and Moulis-en-Médoc
places.note: Two inland communes with no 1855 growth; Chasse-Spleen at Moulis has long been the model of what a cru bourgeois can be, whatever the current list says.

places.name: Haut-Médoc
places.note: The broad appellation around the communes, with La Lagune and Cantemerle classed in 1855 and Sociando-Mallet unclassified.

places.name: Graves
places.note: The gravel south of the city along the Garonne, the oldest Bordeaux vineyard: red and dry white, with Graves Supérieures and Cérons for sweet wine.

places.name: Pessac-Léognan
places.note: Carved from the northern Graves in 1987, holding Haut-Brion and all sixteen crus classés of 1959: smoky reds and barrel-aged whites from Carbonnieux, Domaine de Chevalier, Haut-Bailly and La Mission Haut-Brion.

places.name: Sauternes and Barsac
places.note: Five communes by the Ciron, Sauternes, Barsac, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac, making botrytised sweet wine only; Yquem stands alone as Premier Cru Supérieur.

places.name: Preignac
places.note: Home of Suduiraut, a Premier Cru of 1855, and of Gilette, which ages its wine for decades in concrete.

places.name: Barsac
places.note: Lower and flatter, on limestone, giving lighter and fresher wines: Climens and Coutet are its Premiers Crus; a Barsac may label as Sauternes.

places.name: Right Bank
places.note: The Libournais, on the right bank of the Dordogne around Libourne: Merlot with Cabernet Franc on clay, limestone and small patches of gravel.

places.name: Saint-Émilion
places.note: The limestone town and plateau: côtes estates such as Ausone, Canon, Pavie and Troplong Mondot on the slopes, graves estates Cheval Blanc and Figeac on gravel beside Pomerol; classified in 1955 and about every decade since, last in 2022.

places.name: The satellites
places.note: Montagne, Lussac, Puisseguin and Saint-Georges hyphenate Saint-Émilion to their own names on cooler land to the north.

places.name: Pomerol
places.note: A small plateau of clay and gravel over an iron pan, blue clay under Pétrus at its crown: Le Pin, Trotanoy, Lafleur, L'Église-Clinet, Vieux Château Certan, Clos L'Église and Bellegrave, none classified.

places.name: Lalande-de-Pomerol
places.note: The satellite north across the Barbanne stream, Merlot-led and softer.

places.name: Fronsac and Canon-Fronsac
places.note: Limestone hills west of Libourne, Merlot of grip and value; Canon-Fronsac is the inner slope.

places.name: Castillon and Francs Côtes de Bordeaux
places.note: The clay-limestone hills east of Saint-Émilion, Merlot-led and the best value on the bank.

places.name: Bourg and Blaye
places.note: Across the Gironde from the Médoc: Côtes de Bourg and Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux, Merlot with a little surviving Malbec.

places.name: Entre-Deux-Mers
places.note: The clay and limestone hills between the Garonne and the Dordogne: dry white under its own name, red sold as Bordeaux.

places.name: Cadillac, Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont
places.note: Three sweet appellations across the river from Sauternes, botrytised Sémillon at a gentler price.

producers.name: Château Lafite Rothschild
producers.why: Pauillac First Growth, the most elegant of the five, cedar and graphite over power.

producers.name: Château Latour
producers.why: Pauillac First Growth by the estuary, the most powerful and longest-lived; left the en primeur system in 2012.

producers.name: Château Margaux
producers.why: First Growth of its commune, perfume and silk, and a white, Pavillon Blanc, sold as Bordeaux Blanc.

producers.name: Château Haut-Brion
producers.why: The Graves First Growth of 1855, the only one outside the Médoc, with a great dry white.

producers.name: Château Mouton Rothschild
producers.why: Promoted to First Growth in 1973, the one change to the 1855 list; artist labels since 1945.

producers.name: Pétrus
producers.why: Pomerol's blue-clay Merlot, the world's most famous wine from that grape, unclassified.

producers.name: Château Cheval Blanc
producers.why: Cabernet Franc-led Saint-Émilion on gravel beside Pomerol; withdrew from the classification before 2022.

producers.name: Château Ausone
producers.why: The limestone côtes of Saint-Émilion at their finest; also withdrew before 2022.

producers.name: Château Figeac
producers.why: Promoted to Premier Grand Cru Classé A in 2022, unusual for its large Cabernet share.

producers.name: Château Pavie
producers.why: The other Premier Grand Cru Classé A of 2022, on the Saint-Émilion côtes.

producers.name: Château d'Yquem
producers.why: Sauternes, the only Premier Cru Supérieur of 1855 and the world's reference sweet wine.

producers.name: Château Climens
producers.why: Barsac Premier Cru made from Sémillon alone, botrytis with freshness.

producers.name: Château Suduiraut
producers.why: Preignac Premier Cru of classic rich Sauternes.

producers.name: Château Cos d'Estournel
producers.why: Saint-Estèphe Second Growth with the pagoda chai, exotic and long-lived.

producers.name: Château Léoville Las Cases
producers.why: The Saint-Julien Second Growth most often called a First in all but name.

producers.name: Château Palmer
producers.why: Margaux Third Growth that outperforms its rank, Merlot-rich and velvety.

producers.name: Château Lynch-Bages
producers.why: Pauillac Fifth Growth of Second Growth stature, the classic cassis and cigar box.

producers.name: Château Carbonnieux
producers.why: Pessac-Léognan cru classé for both colours, the white a textbook barrel-aged Sauvignon and Sémillon.

producers.name: Le Pin
producers.why: A tiny Pomerol whose Merlot became a cult in the 1980s, proof that the bank needs no classification.

exam: The 1855 First Growths with their communes, and Mouton's promotion in 1973.
Left Bank gravel and Cabernet against Right Bank clay and Merlot.
The Médoc communes north to south and each one's signature.
Saint-Émilion's revisable classification and Pomerol's lack of one.
Sauternes: Sémillon, the Ciron, botrytis, Yquem alone at the top.
The white grapes and where they are dry: Pessac-Léognan and Entre-Deux-Mers.
Graves 1959, Cru Bourgeois every five years, and what each label phrase means.
The six legal red grapes, Carmenère and Malbec included.
traps: Haut-Brion is an 1855 First Growth from Pessac-Léognan in the Graves, not the Médoc.
Pomerol has no classification, so Pétrus holds no rank at all.
Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation; Grand Cru Classé is the classification, and the top of it is Premier Grand Cru Classé A.
Sauternes is sweet by law; the estates' dry wines are sold as Bordeaux Blanc.
Entre-Deux-Mers is a white-only appellation despite all the red grown there.
Bordeaux Supérieur means more alcohol and ageing, not a higher class of estate.
Merlot, not Cabernet Sauvignon, is the most planted grape of the whole region.
The Cru Bourgeois list changes every five years; an estate on the 2020 list may be off the 2025 one.

cards.f: The 1855 First Growths and their communes
cards.b: Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild (Pauillac), Margaux (Margaux), Haut-Brion (Pessac-Léognan, Graves). Mouton promoted in 1973.
Left: gravel, Cabernet Sauvignon, Médoc and Graves. Right: clay and limestone, Merlot with Cabernet Franc, Saint-Émilion and Pomerol.

cards.f: The Médoc communes, north to south
cards.b: Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux, with Listrac and Moulis inland; all inside Haut-Médoc.

1855 (Médoc and Sauternes; changed twice: Cantemerle added 1856, Mouton promoted 1973); Graves 1953 and 1959 (one tier); Saint-Émilion (1955, revised about every ten years, last 2022); Cru Bourgeois (every five years); Pomerol none.
The cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne, autumn mists bring botrytis to thin-skinned Sémillon; picked in several tries; at least 45 grams of sugar.
Merlot (most planted), Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère.
Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle, with Sauvignon Gris and a few others; dry at Pessac-Léognan and Entre-Deux-Mers, sweet at Sauternes and Barsac.
Premier Grand Cru Classé A: Figeac and Pavie. Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus withdrew before the revision.

cards.f: Cru Bourgeois du Médoc: the tiers and how often it changes
cards.b: Three tiers since 2020: Cru Bourgeois, Cru Bourgeois Supérieur and Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel. The list is revised every five years, most recently in February 2025, so an estate can join or leave it.
Allowed by the INAO in 2021 for Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur: Arinarnoa, Castets, Marselan, Touriga Nacional, Alvarinho, Liliorila; five per cent of the vineyard, ten per cent of a blend.

questions.q: Which 1855 First Growth lies outside the Médoc, in the Graves?
questions.exp: Haut-Brion in Pessac-Léognan was the only non-Médoc red classified in 1855. Latour and Lafite are Pauillac, Margaux is Margaux.

questions.q: Which château was promoted to First Growth in 1973?
questions.exp: Mouton Rothschild rose from Second to First Growth in 1973, the only promotion the 1855 list has known. Léoville Las Cases remains a Second, Lynch-Bages a Fifth and Palmer a Third.

questions.q: Which Bordeaux appellation has no official classification of its estates?
questions.exp: Pomerol never classified, so Pétrus and Le Pin hold no rank. Saint-Émilion has its own revisable list, and Pauillac and Sauternes estates were ranked in 1855.

questions.q: Which grape is the most widely planted in the whole Bordeaux region?
questions.exp: Merlot covers more of Bordeaux than any other grape, leading the Right Bank and the regional appellations; Cabernet Sauvignon leads only on the Left Bank gravel.

questions.q: Which Bordeaux appellation is reserved for dry white wine alone?
questions.exp: Entre-Deux-Mers covers dry white only, Sauvignon-led and made cold in steel; the red grown between the rivers is sold as Bordeaux or Bordeaux Supérieur. Graves and Pessac-Léognan make both colours.

questions.q: Which cold tributary meets the Garonne in the Sauternes district and brings the mists that breed noble rot?
questions.exp: The spring-fed Ciron runs cold under the forest into the warmer Garonne; the autumn mists where they meet bring botrytis to the Sémillon of Sauternes and Barsac.

questions.q: Which estate alone holds the rank of Premier Cru Supérieur in the 1855 classification of Sauternes?
questions.exp: Yquem was placed alone above the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac in 1855 and has never shared the rank.

questions.q: Which two châteaux hold Premier Grand Cru Classé A in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
questions.exp: The 2022 revision named Figeac, promoted, and Pavie as the two A estates after Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus withdrew from the process.

regions.name: Languedoc-Roussillon
regions.summary: The Languedoc-Roussillon is the Mediterranean arc from the Rhône delta to the Spanish border, the largest vineyard in France and for a century its bulk-wine tank. It now runs on two tracks: IGP Pays d'Oc varietal wines from the plain, and a rising ladder of appellations in the hills where Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and old Carignan grow over garrigue, led by Pic Saint-Loup, Terrasses du Larzac, Faugères, Minervois, Corbières and Fitou. Limoux makes sparkling wine from Mauzac, Picpoul de Pinet the oyster white. Roussillon, under the Pyrenees, is Catalan in spirit and the home of the vins doux naturels: Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes, Grenache or Muscat stopped with spirit.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean throughout: hot, dry summers, mild winters and generous sun, with rain in autumn and spring storms and long droughts between. The winds matter: the tramontane in Roussillon and the western Languedoc and the mistral in the east blow dry and cold, cutting rot and disease so that organic farming is easy, but stressing the vines. The Atlantic reaches the far west around Carcassonne and Limoux, cooling Cabardès and the sparkling vineyards.
terroir.soils: A mosaic. Schist runs through Faugères, the northern half of Saint-Chinian, the Agly valley of Roussillon and the terraces of Banyuls, where its dark surface holds heat for Grenache. Limestone and clay-limestone carry La Clape, Pic Saint-Loup and the southern half of Saint-Chinian; Terrasses du Larzac mixes limestone scree with rounded stones; Minervois and Corbières hold both, with sandstone and marl; the coastal plain is deep alluvium.
terroir.topography: A crescent of plain along the coast rising into the foothills of the Massif Central, the Larzac causse and the Cévennes, the Montagne Noire above the Minervois, the rugged Corbières massif and the Pyrenees over Roussillon, where terraced vineyards drop straight into the sea at Banyuls. Quality follows altitude and slope: coteaux over plain.
terroir.water: The Mediterranean and the lagoons behind it, the Bassin de Thau among them, where Picpoul de Pinet faces the oyster beds of Bouzigues. The Aude, Hérault and Orb flow out of the hills; in Roussillon the Agly, Têt and Tech valleys sort the vineyards.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: Everywhere in the hill blends and the whole basis of Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes, where it is picked very ripe and stopped with spirit.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The improving grape planted since the 1980s, required in most appellation reds and at least half of Pic Saint-Loup: pepper, violet and dark fruit.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Structure and savour on the warm coastal sites, La Clape and Collioure especially; one of the three or four principal grapes of nearly every cru.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: The old workhorse, best from bush vines past fifty years in Faugères, Corbières, Fitou and Roussillon: tannic and rustic unless softened by carbonic maceration.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: Lightness and perfume for rosé and the softer reds; capped in most appellation blends.

grapes.name: Lledoner Pelut
grapes.styles: A downy-leaved cousin of Grenache counted with it in Roussillon and the Languedoc crus.

grapes.name: Mauzac
grapes.styles: The apple-skin grape of Limoux, at least nine tenths of Blanquette de Limoux and all of the méthode ancestrale.

grapes.name: Piquepoul
grapes.styles: The lip-stinger: high-acid, lemony white, the sole grape of Picpoul de Pinet on the lagoon.

grapes.name: Grenache Blanc
grapes.styles: With Grenache Gris, Macabeu, Bourboulenc, Clairette, Roussanne, Marsanne and Vermentino, the white blends of the crus and the ambré styles of Rivesaltes.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Muscat à Petits Grains alone makes the four Languedoc Muscats of Frontignan, Lunel, Mireval and Saint-Jean-de-Minervois; with Muscat of Alexandria it makes Muscat de Rivesaltes.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Limoux's barrel-fermented still white and the lead of Crémant de Limoux, and the biggest white of IGP Pays d'Oc.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: A partner of Chardonnay in Limoux still white and Crémant de Limoux, bringing acidity.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted grape of the IGP Pays d'Oc plain, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc, in varietal wines for export.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: An Atlantic grape blended with Mediterranean varieties in Cabardès and with Merlot in Malepère near Carcassonne, and a varietal on the plain.

wines.note: Syrah-led with Grenache and Mourvèdre from the cooler hills north of Montpellier: fresh, peppery, garrigue-scented; red and rosé only.
Carignan-based reds of the rugged south-west: Boutenac is the cru of Corbières, Fitou the oldest red appellation of the Languedoc, 1948, in two zones.
Piquepoul alone from the shore of the Bassin de Thau: lemon, salt and high acid, poured with the oysters of Bouzigues.
Mauzac-based Blanquette by the traditional method, claiming 1531 as the first sparkling wine; Crémant leads with Chardonnay and Chenin and is the finer.
Red only, from the Agly hills and Les Aspres to the south-west: Grenache, Syrah, Carignan and Mourvèdre, warm and mineral; five communes may add their names.
The dry wine of the Banyuls terraces: Grenache and Mourvèdre reds of sun and salt, rosé and white; a grower chooses yearly between Collioure and Banyuls.
Grenache vin doux naturel from the sea terraces: young and reductive as rimage, or aged in old wood and glass bonbonnes to rancio; the chocolate wine.
Grenache vin doux naturel from the black schist of the upper Agly, deeper and more tannic than Banyuls; dry red Maury Sec since 2011.
The broad Roussillon vin doux naturel in ambré, tuilé, grenat and hors d'âge styles, caramel and walnut with age; Muscat de Rivesaltes is fresh and grapey.
France's largest IGP: varietal wines from the plain, Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Viognier, clean and ripe, priced for the glass.

made.viticulture: Two vineyards share the arc. On the plain, vines are wire trained, machine pruned and machine picked, irrigation is allowed under the IGP rules in dry years, and yields run high for varietal wine. In the hills the old way survives: Carignan and Grenache as bush vines, en gobelet, low against the tramontane and the mistral, many of them over fifty years old, with Syrah and Mourvèdre on wires beside them; the appellations fix low yields and require blends of at least two principal grapes. The dry wind keeps mildew and rot rare, which has made this one of France's largest organic vineyards, and the hazards are drought, water stress, heat spikes at véraison, hail and summer fire in the garrigue. Harvest starts in August for the Muscats and the sparkling base and runs into October for Mourvèdre and Carignan. Vine-pull schemes since the 1980s took out much of the bulk vineyard, and the coteaux were replanted to the Rhône grapes.
made.winemaking: The hill reds are destemmed or part whole bunch and fermented in concrete, steel or large wood; Carignan is often given carbonic maceration to tame its tannin and bring out fruit, and the finished blend is aged in old foudre or barrique. Cooperatives still make much of the volume, and the IGP wines are made cold and clean in steel for export. Picpoul is made cold in steel, Limoux's Chardonnay in barrel. Blanquette and Crémant de Limoux go through the traditional method with a second fermentation in bottle; the méthode ancestrale bottles Mauzac before its first fermentation is finished, so it finishes sweet and low in alcohol. The vins doux naturels are made by mutage: during fermentation, when the must is still rich in sugar, five to ten per cent of neutral grape spirit at 96 per cent is added and the yeast stops, leaving sweetness and 15 to 18 per cent alcohol; the must needs at least 252 grams of sugar per litre. Grenat and rimage are bottled young; ambré, tuilé, rancio and hors d'âge age for years in old casks and glass bonbonnes left out in the sun.

law.classification: The base is Vin de France, then the IGPs: Pays d'Oc for the whole region and the departmental ones, Hérault, Aude, Gard and Côtes Catalanes among them. AOC Languedoc, renamed from Coteaux du Languedoc in 2007, is the regional appellation from Nîmes to the Spanish border and may carry a named sub-zone such as Pézenas. Above it the crus hold their own appellations: Faugères and Saint-Chinian (1982), Minervois and Corbières (1985), Fitou (1948), Picpoul de Pinet (2013), Terrasses du Larzac (2014), La Clape (2015), Pic Saint-Loup (2017), and the two village crus, Minervois-La Livinière (1999) and Corbières-Boutenac (2005), both now under their own names, La Livinière and Boutenac, approved by the European Union in March 2024; Montpeyroux, inside the Terrasses du Larzac, was approved by the INAO in June 2025 as a red-only appellation, from the 2026 vintage. Roussillon climbs from Côtes du Roussillon to Côtes du Roussillon Villages with five named communes, with Collioure for dry wine, and Banyuls, Banyuls Grand Cru, Maury and Rivesaltes for the fortified wines.
tiers: Vin de France and IGP
Pays d'Oc is the great varietal IGP; departmental IGPs include Hérault, Aude, Gard and Côtes Catalanes.
AOC Languedoc
The regional appellation, with named sub-zones such as Grés de Montpellier and Pézenas on the label.
The crus with their own appellation

Pic Saint-Loup, Terrasses du Larzac, La Clape, Picpoul de Pinet, Faugères, Saint-Chinian, Minervois, Corbières, Fitou, Cabardès, Malepère, Clairette du Languedoc, Montpeyroux (approved 2025, from the 2026 vintage).
The village crus
La Livinière inside Minervois (1999) and Boutenac inside Corbières (2005), both now labelled under their own names, a change the European Union approved in March 2024.
Limoux
Blanquette de Limoux (Mauzac at least 90 per cent), Blanquette méthode ancestrale (Mauzac alone), Crémant de Limoux (Chardonnay and Chenin lead), Limoux still white and red.
Côtes du Roussillon and Côtes du Roussillon Villages
Villages is red only, from the northern hills and Les Aspres, with Caramany, Latour-de-France, Lesquerde, Tautavel and Les Aspres as named communes.
Collioure
The dry red, rosé and white of the Banyuls zone.
Vins doux naturels

Banyuls (Grenache Noir at least 50 per cent), Banyuls Grand Cru (at least 75 per cent, 30 months in wood), Maury, Rivesaltes, Muscat de Rivesaltes, Muscat de Frontignan, Lunel, Mireval and Saint-Jean-de-Minervois.
labels: A sweet wine whose fermentation was stopped by adding grape spirit; the sweetness is the grape's own
A vintage vin doux naturel bottled young without oxidative ageing: rimage at Banyuls, grenat at Rivesaltes and Maury
Oxidatively aged red and white vins doux naturels of Rivesaltes and Maury
A nutty, oxidised style from long ageing in warmth and air
A vin doux naturel aged at least five years
Bottled before the first fermentation ends; Blanquette de Limoux's gently sweet version
The IGP of the whole region, varietal labelling allowed
A regional marketing banner, not a legal category
A very pale rosé pressed from grey-skinned grapes on the sandy coast

places.name: Languedoc
places.note: From Nîmes past Montpellier, Béziers and Narbonne to Carcassonne: the plain for IGP, the hills for the crus.

places.name: Pic Saint-Loup
places.note: The limestone peak and cooler hills north of Montpellier, an appellation of its own since 2017 for red and rosé, Syrah at least half the blend.

places.name: Terrasses du Larzac
places.note: The limestone foothills under the causse, red only since 2014, with cool nights for freshness; Mas Jullien at Jonquières is the standard.

places.name: Montpeyroux
places.note: A village of the Terrasses whose own red-only appellation the INAO approved in June 2025, from the 2026 vintage.

places.name: Aniane
places.note: Where Mas de Daumas Gassac and the Grange des Pères showed from 1978 and 1992 what the Languedoc could do, both bottled as IGP.

places.name: Grés de Montpellier, Pézenas and Saint-Georges-d'Orques
places.note: Named sub-zones of AOC Languedoc on the label after the regional name, a rung below the crus.

places.name: Picpoul de Pinet
places.note: The shore of the Bassin de Thau lagoon at Pinet, Piquepoul alone, an appellation since 2013; Bouzigues oysters across the water.

places.name: Faugères
places.note: Schist hills north of Béziers, an appellation since 1982: tense, smoky reds from Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and old Carignan.

places.name: Saint-Chinian
places.note: Beside Faugères, schist in the north and clay-limestone in the south, since 1982; Berlou and Roquebrun are named villages from 2005.

places.name: La Clape
places.note: A limestone massif by Narbonne that was once an island, hot, dry and windy; its own appellation since 2015, red and Bourboulenc-led white.

places.name: Minervois
places.note: Terraces under the Montagne Noire west of Béziers, an appellation since 1985, spiced Syrah and Grenache blends.

places.name: La Livinière
places.note: The first village cru of the Languedoc, 1999, and since March 2024 labelled under its own name, Minervois dropped; structured, age-worthy reds.

places.name: Corbières
places.note: The rugged massif south of Narbonne, the largest appellation of the Languedoc since 1985, Carignan-based reds with some white and rosé.

places.name: Boutenac
places.note: The Corbières cru of 2005 around old-vine Carignan, labelled as Boutenac alone since the EU approved the change in March 2024.

places.name: Fitou
places.note: The Languedoc's oldest red appellation, 1948, in two zones, the coast at Fitou and Leucate and the high Corbières; Carignan-based red only.

places.name: Cabardès and Malepère
places.note: Near Carcassonne: Cabardès blends Atlantic Cabernet and Merlot with Syrah and Grenache, Malepère leads with Merlot.

places.name: Limoux
places.note: The upper Aude valley south of Carcassonne, cool enough for sparkling wine; the abbey of Saint-Hilaire claims a Blanquette in 1531; four appellations.

places.name: The Muscats of the coast
places.note: Frontignan, Mireval and Lunel near Montpellier and Saint-Jean-de-Minervois in the hills: Muscat à Petits Grains vins doux naturels.

places.name: Roussillon
places.note: The Pyrénées-Orientales around Perpignan, split by the Agly, Têt and Tech valleys and swept by the tramontane: vins doux naturels and dry wines from very old vines.

places.name: Agly valley and Calce
places.note: The schist and limestone hills of the north, home of four of the five Villages communes, where Domaine Gauby at Calce made old-vine Grenache and Carignan famous.

places.name: Maury
places.note: The upper Agly valley on black schist: Grenache vins doux naturels, deeper than Banyuls, and dry red Maury Sec since 2011.

places.name: Rivesaltes
places.note: The town north of Perpignan that names the broad vin doux naturel appellation and Muscat de Rivesaltes.

places.name: Banyuls and Collioure
places.note: Terraced schist falling to the sea at the border: the same vines give Banyuls when fortified and Collioure when dry.

places.name: Les Aspres
places.note: The foothills south-west of Perpignan, a named commune of Côtes du Roussillon Villages since 2017.

producers.name: Mas de Daumas Gassac
producers.why: The Aniane estate whose Cabernet-led red from the 1970s first proved the Languedoc could make a great wine, sold as IGP.

producers.name: Domaine de la Grange des Pères
producers.why: Aniane's cult neighbour, Syrah, Mourvèdre and Cabernet aged long in barrel, bottled as IGP.

producers.name: Mas Jullien
producers.why: The benchmark of Terrasses du Larzac at Jonquières, fresh and precise hill reds.

producers.name: Domaine Léon Barral
producers.why: Faugères schist farmed with cattle between the rows and no plough, the reference for Carignan and Syrah from that soil.

producers.name: Domaine Gauby
producers.why: Calce in the Agly valley, the estate that put dry Roussillon from old vines on the world's lists.

producers.name: Mas Amiel
producers.why: The great Maury estate, vins doux naturels aged in glass bonbonnes in the sun and serious dry reds.

producers.name: Domaine de la Rectorie
producers.why: Banyuls-sur-Mer grower making both Banyuls and Collioure from the sea terraces.

producers.name: Domaine La Tour Vieille
producers.why: Collioure estate whose Banyuls Reserva and dry reds show the two faces of one vineyard.

producers.name: Riveyrac
producers.why: A Rivesaltes house releasing vins doux naturels from single old vintages after decades in cask.

exam: The crus with their own appellation and what each is known for: Pic Saint-Loup, Terrasses du Larzac, La Clape, Faugères, Saint-Chinian, Minervois, Corbières, Fitou.
Picpoul de Pinet as the oyster white and its single grape.
Limoux: Blanquette from Mauzac, Crémant from Chardonnay and Chenin, the 1531 claim.
The vin doux naturel method, mutage, and the Roussillon names: Banyuls, Maury, Rivesaltes.
Collioure as the dry wine of the Banyuls vineyard.
IGP Pays d'Oc as the varietal engine and the largest IGP in France.
Fitou as the oldest red appellation and its two zones.
The recent changes: La Livinière and Boutenac under their own names from 2024, Montpeyroux approved in 2025.
traps: Fitou lies inside Corbières country and predates it as an appellation: 1948 against 1985.
Picpoul de Pinet is a white from Piquepoul; Pinet is the village, not a grape.
Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes are fortified sweet wines; Collioure and Maury Sec are the dry wines of the same ground.
Muscat de Rivesaltes may use Muscat of Alexandria; the four Languedoc Muscats use Muscat à Petits Grains alone.
Blanquette de Limoux is Mauzac-based and the Crémant is Chardonnay and Chenin-led; both are traditional method, only the méthode ancestrale is not.
Pic Saint-Loup makes no white under its own name; La Clape does.
Terrasses du Larzac is red only; Faugères and Saint-Chinian make all three colours.
Vin doux naturel is not naturally sweet wine in the Sauternes sense: the sugar is kept by adding spirit.

cards.b: A sweet wine whose fermentation is stopped by adding neutral grape spirit (mutage), keeping the grape's own sugar; 15 to 18 per cent alcohol; Grenache or Muscat.
Banyuls and Banyuls Grand Cru (sea terraces), Maury (upper Agly schist), Rivesaltes (the broad one), Muscat de Rivesaltes.
The same terraced vineyard at the Spanish border: fortified and sweet as Banyuls, dry red, rosé or white as Collioure.
Traditional method sparkling from at least 90 per cent Mauzac in the upper Aude; the abbey of Saint-Hilaire claims 1531. Crémant de Limoux leads with Chardonnay and Chenin.
Piquepoul alone from the Bassin de Thau lagoon: lemon, salt, high acid; the oyster wine of Bouzigues; an appellation since 2013.
The oldest red appellation of the Languedoc, 1948, Carignan-based, in two zones: the coast at Fitou and Leucate, and the high Corbières.
Cooler hills north of Montpellier; its own appellation since 2017; red and rosé only; Syrah at least half.

cards.f: The named communes of Côtes du Roussillon Villages
cards.b: Caramany, Latour-de-France, Lesquerde, Tautavel and Les Aspres (2017); the Villages appellation is red only.

cards.f: The Languedoc crus with their own appellation
cards.b: Pic Saint-Loup, Terrasses du Larzac, La Clape, Picpoul de Pinet, Faugères, Saint-Chinian, Minervois, Corbières, Fitou, Cabardès, Malepère, Limoux, Montpeyroux (approved 2025).

cards.f: Recent changes in the Languedoc ladder
cards.b: La Livinière and Boutenac stand under their own names, the EU approving the changes in March 2024; Montpeyroux approved by the INAO in June 2025, red only, from the 2026 vintage.

questions.q: Which white grape alone makes the appellation wine grown on the shore of the Bassin de Thau?
questions.exp: Picpoul de Pinet, on the shore of the Bassin de Thau, is Piquepoul Blanc alone, the high-acid lip-stinger. Bourboulenc leads La Clape white, Clairette has its own Languedoc appellation and Mauzac is Limoux's grape.

questions.q: Which is the oldest red wine appellation of the Languedoc, dating from 1948?
questions.exp: Fitou was granted its appellation in 1948, decades before Faugères (1982) and Corbières and Minervois (1985), and lies in two zones within Corbières country.

questions.q: Which grape must make up at least 90 per cent of Blanquette de Limoux?
questions.exp: Blanquette de Limoux is built on Mauzac, at least nine tenths; Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc lead the Crémant de Limoux instead, and Clairette has no part in either.

questions.q: What is the French term for stopping the fermentation of a vin doux naturel by adding grape spirit?
questions.exp: Mutage is the addition of neutral spirit to the fermenting must, which kills the yeast and keeps the sugar. Saignée draws off rosé juice, remuage riddles sparkling wine and débourbage settles juice.

questions.q: Which Roussillon vin doux naturel comes from terraces falling to the sea at the Spanish border, with Collioure as its dry counterpart?
questions.exp: Banyuls is the Grenache vin doux naturel of the schist terraces at the border; the same vines, vinified dry, are sold as Collioure.

questions.q: Which village inside Minervois became the first cru of the Languedoc in 1999?
questions.exp: Minervois-La Livinière was the first village-level cru of the Languedoc in 1999, and in March 2024 the European Union approved its change of name to La Livinière alone.

questions.q: Under which regional IGP is most of the varietal wine of the Languedoc-Roussillon sold?
questions.exp: IGP Pays d'Oc, the former Vin de Pays d'Oc of 1987, is the largest IGP in France and the label on most of the region's varietal Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah, Chardonnay and Sauvignon.

questions.q: Which red-only Languedoc appellation was created in 2014 on the limestone foothills below the causse?
questions.exp: Terrasses du Larzac gained its own appellation in 2014 for red wine alone, Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre and Carignan from the cool foothills south of the Cévennes.
